title: Real-time 3×3 Convolution Processor
summary: Streaming grayscale filter (sharpen / blur), one pixel per clock. The accumulator is built twice, as a combinational adder tree and as a 9-PE systolic chain, then compared on Vivado resources and Fmax at three image sizes.
imageAlt: Block diagram: line buffer, 3×3 window, convolution core, output
body: Pixels stream in through i_pixel. A two-row line_buffer and window_3x3 form a 3×3 window every clock. The convolution core multiplies the window by the kernel chosen by mode and accumulates the 9 products. Only that core differs between the two versions; the line buffer, window and output stage are shared.
Kernels: sharpen [0 −1 0; −1 5 −1; 0 −1 0], clipped to [0, 255]. Blur adds the 9 pixels and approximates ÷9 as (sum × 114) >>> 10.
Clock constraint 5.5 ns for every run. Fmax = 1 / (T − WNS). Two runs miss the constraint by 2 ps and 13 ps.

The systolic version costs 2.3–2.9× the LUTs, mostly in the shift_delay chains that keep each PE on the same window. Its Fmax is no better, because both cores share the blur scaling stage, which is the likely critical path. At 3×3 the adder tree is only 4 levels deep; the systolic advantage should appear at 5×5 or 7×7.

golden_model.py reproduces the RTL arithmetic. After compensating the pipeline fill offset, RTL output matches it on 97.2 % (64×64) to 99.2 % (256×256) of pixels in both modes and both architectures. The mismatches are at the image border: the line buffer has no edge handling.
Simulation and Vivado reports only, not run on a board.
No border handling: the first two rows are computed against reset values.

title: AM Modulator with Dual NCOs
summary: Pipelined DSB-FC amplitude modulator built on two 32-bit phase-accumulator NCOs. Compares full-wave and quarter-wave sine ROMs at AW = 8, 10 and 12, with every configuration verified bit-exact.
imageAlt: AM modulator block diagram: carrier and message NCOs, envelope, multiplier
body: Each NCO is a 32-bit accumulator whose top AW bits address a 12-bit sine table, giving 0.023 Hz resolution at 100 MHz. The envelope is amp_car + (amp_msg · msg) >>> 11 and the output is (env · car) >>> 11. Every stage is registered, so the critical path is a single multiply.
The quarter-wave ROM stores 2<sup>AW−2</sup> words and rebuilds the period by mirroring the address and negating the sample. A half-sample offset in the table makes this reconstruction exact.
tb_am_top: 7 self-checks, including 10 000 samples bit-exact against an in-testbench reference.
Python golden model: 18 / 18 regression cases × 10 000 samples, compared with no offset search.
Overflow ruled out by an exhaustive sweep of every legal input (24 Python unit tests).
SFDR rises about 6 dB per address bit, as phase-truncation theory predicts, and is identical for full and quarter ROMs.
Simulation and implementation only. No board, no DAC.
Overmodulation (μ > 1) is not limited or flagged.

title: 4-Channel TDM Mux / Demux
summary: Four 8-bit channels serialised over one wire in 32-clock frames. A single 5-bit counter times both sides; there is no FSM and no handshake.
specs: 33 clk after reset · ≤ 41 clk after a change
imageAlt: TDM block diagram: mux, TX shift register, serial line, RX shift register, demux, shared counter
body: Each byte takes 8 clocks, MSB first, and a frame is CH0 → CH3 in 32 clocks. The free-running bit_count is the only timing reference, so the receiver always knows which channel a finished byte belongs to without sync bits.
Because the shift registers load on the next edge, tdm_top adds a small glue layer that realigns load and capture. With it, outputs match inputs exactly once the pipeline has filled.
System testbench: 38 / 38 checks on both Icarus Verilog and Vivado XSIM.
Python golden model: 200 / 200 random vectors match on stream, outputs and latency.

title: Offline Keyword Spotting on a Custom ESP32 Board
summary: Our own ESP32-WROOM-32UE board with an INMP441 I²S microphone. A 22-class 1D-CNN, quantised to int8, runs entirely on the chip and shows the word and its confidence on an OLED. No Wi-Fi at run time.
imageAlt: System block diagram: microphone, ESP32, OLED and LEDs
body: The firmware is a single superloop. A button press records 1 s at 16 kHz over I²S, removes DC offset, extracts MFE features (25 ms frames, 32 Mel filters, 3136 features) and runs the CNN (Conv16 → Conv32 → Dense128 → 22). The top class goes to the OLED, serial log and status LEDs.
Training data was recorded with the same microphone on an ESP32-S3 kit using our capture firmware and a push-to-talk recorder, then extended with synthetic speech.
A rejection threshold: the top class is always shown.
Bringing the KiCad schematic in line with the fabricated PCB.
